The Gen Z brief: what India's 377 million want from a screen

They are 57% of the Hindi box office and 70% of every opening day. They spend four hours a day inside a feed built to keep them there. They cried at Saiyaara, quoted Dhurandhar, and are telling R. Madhavan's son they would rather watch anime. This is who they are, how they decide, and what Bollywood still has that nothing else does.

PUBLISHED 21 AUGUST 2026 · BOXOFFY AUDIENCE INTELLIGENCE · ~26 MIN READ

  1. Who they are: size, money, and seventeen very different cities
  2. Where the hours go: screens, feeds, reels
  3. Attention, second screens and what "short attention span" actually means

  10. The Boxoffy read: twelve things to change on Monday

Every few months somebody in the Hindi film industry says the young audience has left. R. Madhavan said it in July, about his own son's generation: they are watching Korean dramas and Japanese anime, they do not want Hindi or Tamil films, many do not want to go to theatres at all. The numbers say something more precise, and more useful. The young audience has not left. It has become the only audience that reliably shows up on day one, and it is showing up on its own terms.

This brief is written for the people who greenlight films. It is a profile rather than a manifesto. Where a number exists, we give it and say where it came from. Where we are reading between the lines, we say that too.

01Who they are

377M
Gen Z population in India — the largest generation the country has ever had (Snap & BCG)
$860B
spending they directly drive or influence — 43% of national consumption (Snap & BCG, 2024)
57%
of Hindi box office revenue comes from under-30s (Ormax TOBAR 2026)
70%
of first-day box office is under-30 (Ormax TOBAR 2026)

Three facts frame everything else. First, scale: at 377 million, India's Gen Z is larger than the entire population of the United States. Second, money: $860 billion in spending driven directly or through household influence, with direct spend alone expected to reach $250 billion in 2025 and $1.8 trillion by 2035. One in four is already earning; within a decade it will be one in two. Third, the bit that matters for a greenlight meeting: under-30s are 57% of the Hindi box office and 70% of opening day. The segment the trade spent a decade worrying about losing is the segment that now decides whether a film opens.

That 70% figure deserves a pause. Opening day is the number the trade reports, the number that sets the narrative, the number that drives the second-weekend hold. If seven in ten of those tickets are bought by people under thirty, then opening-day box office in India is, functionally, a Gen Z verdict.

Where they are

The Snap-BCG work is urban-weighted, but the more interesting signal comes from short-video platforms: FICCI-EY found that 68% of short-video consumers are in tier-two cities — Bhubaneswar, Jaipur, Kanpur, Kota, Patna — where the format is twice as popular as in tier-one. This is the audience that single screens used to serve and multiplexes have priced out. They are not gone. They have moved their attention to a phone.

Treating that as one audience is the mistake. A twenty-year-old in Gurgaon and a twenty-year-old in Kanpur are the same generation and not remotely the same customer. One has IMAX within an hour and a recliner habit; the other has a single-screen ticket at a third the price and a phone that already gives him everything else. The seventeen markets below cover the spread, from the five cities that lead BookMyShow ticket sales down to the single-screen belt.

How to read this. The four bars are a Boxoffy index, 0–100, built from inputs we can verify per market: premium-format availability (India’s 30-plus IMAX screens sit in Mumbai, Delhi, Noida, Gurugram, Bengaluru, Chennai, Pune and Ahmedabad — not one tier-two city on this board has one), local ATP bands, surviving single-screen share, dominant language, and FICCI-EY’s finding that short-video consumption runs twice as high in tier two as tier one. BookMyShow flags reflect the platform’s own disclosures: Mumbai, Delhi-NCR, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Chennai lead ticket sales, the top ten cities account for 48% of them, and Coimbatore and Kochi have both outsold Kolkata. This is a model, not a survey. No public research segments Indian Gen Z cinema behaviour city by city; if one is published we will grade this against it.
Share the map WhatsAppXFacebookTelegram

The diagonal is the whole finding. Premium-format appetite and price sensitivity move against each other almost perfectly, which means a single national release strategy is wrong for most of this board. The useful cases sit off the line.

Bengaluru and Kochi are the outliers that matter most, for the same reason: both score far higher on subtitle comfort than their ticket price predicts. Kochi reads subtitles by default; Bengaluru will watch the Kannada original, the Tamil dub and the English print of one film. Neither is a market you dub down to. Hyderabad, Chennai and Vijayawada invert it — real premium appetite paired with low subtitle tolerance, which is why a Telugu track can outsell a Tamil one on the same title in the same week.

Then there is the gap between a city's size and its sales. Kolkata is a metro that BookMyShow's own numbers show being outsold by Coimbatore and Kochi, neither of them close to it in population. Ahmedabad is the platform's stand-out growth market and barely features in Hindi release planning. And Bhopal is the quiet rebuttal to the ticket-price panic: its ATP rose 26% since 2019 against 41% in Mumbai and Delhi, which is why the affordability argument sounds completely different depending on which city is having it.

Jaipur, Bhubaneswar, Indore, Bhopal and Kanpur carry the five highest reel-led discovery scores on the board and do not have one IMAX screen between them. That is an audience a song can deliver and a premium format cannot.

What this means for a producer

Your opening-day audience is concentrated, young, and urban-plus-tier-two. It researches 1.5× more than millennials before spending. Seventy percent of it relies on an inner circle for guidance and shares updates. It does not discover your film through a trailer on television. It discovers it through YouTube, Instagram and BookMyShow, in that order. (Ormax TOBAR 2026.)

02Where the hours go

Globally, Gen Z logs around four hours a day on social platforms and close to nine hours of total screen time. India-specific figures are harder to pin, but the shape is consistent across sources: phone-first, video-first, short-form-first.

Two of those rows cut against the mobile-only caricature and are worth more attention than they will get. Indian Gen Z is spending 3.1 hours a day on connected television, and 77% of that viewing is with friends or family. Many are "cord-nevers" who started their television life on a smart TV with no memory of linear. The big screen at home is not dead for this generation. It is the first screen they ever knew.

The other is the reels figure. Forty to sixty percent of a young Indian's screen time on content under a minute long, at a rate of several hundred clips per sitting, is not a viewing habit. It is a dopamine schedule. Anything you put in front of them competes with that baseline.

They have a nine-hour screen day. You want two and a half hours of it, in a room they have to travel to, at a price. That is the ask.

03Attention, second screens, and the "short attention span" myth

The lazy version of the thesis is that Gen Z cannot concentrate. The data is more specific and more actionable.

Second-screening is near-universal and mostly benign

Eighty-eight percent of Indian Gen Z connected-TV viewers exhibit two-screen behaviour — phone in hand while the big screen plays. Globally, 76% of Gen Z use their phone while watching TV, and roughly 85% scroll social media during viewing. But Omdia's 2025 work found that Gen Z's second-screen rate has plateaued at around 63%, while it is the over-45s whose multitasking is now growing fastest. In other words, the generation everyone worried about has settled into a stable pattern; it is their parents who are changing.

What the phone is doing matters. The Indian CTV research says it is "discovery and engagement" — looking up the actor, sharing a clip, checking who else is watching. The phone is a companion to the content more often than a competitor to it. Canvas8 found Gen Z is most likely to second-screen during shows they have already seen. New material still gets the full screen.

What "attention span" actually means here

Fifty-five percent of Gen Z adults say they prefer videos under 15 minutes to long-form — but that is preference in the abstract, not behaviour with something they care about. The same cohort went to cinemas 6.1 times a year in the US in 2025, up from 4.9, the highest of any age group, and sat through a three-hour Odyssey in 70mm IMAX. The better framing is not attention span but attention threshold: the bar for earning the first ninety seconds is brutally high, and once cleared, the capacity for long-form is intact.

The operating rule

You are not competing with a short attention span. You are competing with a very well-tuned detector for insincerity that has seen 400 reels today and can tell within seconds whether a thing is trying. Earn the first scene and they will give you three hours. Lose it and they are on the phone before the title card.

04What they watch instead of you

Madhavan's diagnosis was correct in its particulars. The alternatives are real, and each one is winning on a specific axis.

Anime

Across seven markets including India, 44% of respondents identified as anime fans — more than K-drama, more than Bollywood. Among Gen Z it was 54%: more than BTS, more than the NFL. In the US, Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle sold 42% of its tickets to Gen Z, the highest share of any 2025 release. Anime wins on serialised world-building, unapologetic sincerity, and characters who suffer visibly for what they want. It is also fully available, fully subtitled, and fully legal on the platforms they already use.

K-drama

K-content wins on emotional precision and production gloss at a consistent standard. The romance is earnest, the leads are beautiful, the pacing is patient in a way Bollywood used to be and stopped being. When THR India asked what romance the young ones have today, the answer was that DDLJ belonged to the '90s and Rockstar to the generation after — and then nothing, until Saiyaara filled the gap. K-drama had been filling it in the meantime.

Hollywood

Spider-Man: Brand New Day did ₹334.70 Cr net in its first eight days in India, and the English version out-earned the Hindi dub by ₹63 Cr. That is a metro-multiplex, premium-format, original-language audience — and it is young. Hollywood wins on spectacle that is reliably delivered and IP they grew up inside. A Minecraft Movie was the most-attended film by Gen Z in the US in 2025 because it was the game they played at nine.

Micro-drama and reels

India's micro-drama market crossed $300 million in its first year with 100 million MAUs and 450 million downloads (Lumikai). Projections run to $4.5 billion by 2030. These are one-to-three-minute episodes, vertical, cliffhanger-driven, and the Indian audience takes to them because they are structurally a soap opera at 50× speed. They win on zero friction and instant closure. As we argued in the microdrama brief, this is competition for the mobile-gaming hour, not the cinema hour — but it is training the palate.

OTT originals

The streamers win on darker themes, ensemble casts and the absence of a star system. Reema Kagti's complaint that algorithmic success has replaced the box office as the yardstick, producing homogeneity, is a real problem for OTT — but from the audience's side it still looks like more variety than the theatrical Hindi slate offers.

05How they decide on a ticket

Ormax's TOBAR 2026 segments India's 28.5 million regular urban Hindi cinema-goers into five groups. The largest, 35%, is the RARE crowd — people who come out only for event films with real public conversation behind them. Gen Z overlaps heavily with this segment and with what Ormax calls Spectacle and Story Seekers: if a film does not offer both, they wait for streaming.

The discovery funnel

Top three marketing sources, in order: YouTube, Instagram, online ticketing apps (BookMyShow first, then District). In-theatre advertising is fourth. Television does not make the list.

The triggers

  • Social proof, loudly. Forty percent of audiences share film-related memes after watching. The RARE crowd moves when it sees a conversation it is not part of yet.
  • The song before the film. Saiyaara's title track passed 400 million YouTube views; Dhurandhar's entry theme and its Arijit track were the film's cultural afterlife. For this generation music isn't promotion. It's the product's first release.
  • The group. Going to the cinema is a social activity for Gen Z in a way it is not for their parents. Fandango's 2026 study found Gen Z is now the most frequent cinemagoing cohort at roughly seven visits a year, citing the shared experience and "a reason to leave the house." Indian Gen Z watches CTV with others 77% of the time. They do not go alone.
  • Premium if the film earns it. Gen Z over-indexes on IMAX and PLF upgrades when the film is an event. Spider-Man's English-version dominance in India is premium-format behaviour.

The barriers

Here is the finding that surprised Ormax's own researchers: the biggest barrier to more frequent cinema-going is not ticket price. It is overpriced food and beverage. India's average ticket price rose 47% from ₹91 in 2020 to ₹134 in 2024 and then flattened; a young audience has absorbed that. What it resents is a ₹400 popcorn-and-cola that costs more than the seat. This is an exhibitor problem, but it is the studio's opening weekend that pays for it.

The decision, compressed

A song lands on Instagram. The group chat decides. Someone checks BookMyShow for the nearest PLF screen. Memes from the first shows arrive by Friday night. If they are good, the RARE crowd buys for Saturday. If they are not, the film is on the phone by week two and nobody is coming.

06What they read

The panic about Gen Z and books gets the direction wrong. US-representative data across 2020, 2022 and 2025 shows 66% of Gen Z now identify as readers, up fourteen points; 65% read a print book in the past year, up from 59%. What changed is how: multimodally, bouncing between print, e-book and audiobook for the same title, and on platforms older surveys do not count — Wattpad, Webtoon, manga, fan fiction, BookTok.

We do not have an India-specific equivalent and will not invent one. But the Wattpad and Webtoon numbers are global and India is one of their largest markets. The structural finding travels: this generation reads serialised, character-driven, emotionally maximalist fiction in enormous volume — it just reads it on a phone, often written by someone its own age.

The relevance for a writers' room is direct. The most-read fiction among this cohort is romance and fantasy with high emotional stakes, unembarrassed sincerity, and protagonists who are flawed in ways the reader recognises. Perfect Addiction, a kickboxing romance on Wattpad, has 85.6 million reads. That is the taste Saiyaara served, and it is the taste Bollywood's A-list screenwriters have been told for a decade is uncool.

They are not reading less. They are reading things that make them feel more, written by people who are not ashamed of that.

07What they want from a character

This is the section producers actually need, so we will be blunt.

The vocabulary, decoded

WordWhat it actually meansWhat kills it
VibeA coherent emotional atmosphere that does not break. The film knows what it is and stays there.Tonal lurches. A comedy set-piece in a tragedy. An item song that stops the story.
DripVisual self-possession. Costume, posture and framing that say the character chose to look this way.Stylists dressing for the poster. Anyone who looks like they are wearing a brand deal.
CringeThe gap between how hard something is trying to land and how well it lands. Detectable instantly.Dialogue written to be quotable. Youth slang written by someone over forty. Forced relatability.
AuraUnspoken authority. The character who does not need to explain himself.Characters who narrate their own coolness.
RealThe character has a cost. Wanting something visibly hurts them.Heroes who win without losing anything.

The authenticity test, and why nepotism is a symptom not the disease

The nepotism debate is loud and mostly misdirected. Gen Z does not reject star kids on principle — Saiyaara's male lead is a Panday and the film did ₹270 Cr net in twelve days. What they reject is unearned confidence on screen: an actor who has not been made to work for the frame, written by a team that assumes the surname does the work. Gulf News' observation that the current crop "look and sound alike" is a casting note, not a politics note. The audience can tell when a performance was built and when it was handed over.

The Deloitte data on what this cohort wants from work transfers directly to what it wants from characters: 99% say purpose matters, roughly half have turned down an assignment on principle, 48% have rejected an employer over values, and 46% have taken time off for stress. They want protagonists who have a reason, who pay a price for it, and who are allowed to be visibly not-okay. The stoic Bollywood hero who feels nothing and wins everything reads as a lie to a generation that has normalised talking about anxiety.

Who they actually attach to

The clearest Indian example is in Dhurandhar. Young viewers did not obsess over the hero. They obsessed over Rehman Dakait — Akshaye Khanna's morally grey antagonist with a wife, a family, and humanity written into the violence. That is the anime instinct: the character who is dangerous and tender, who has a cost, whose entry music you can cut a reel to. Bollywood has historically written the villain thin and the hero flat. Gen Z wants the opposite.

The three questions a Gen Z viewer asks a character

1. What do you want? Stated or not, it has to be legible in scene one.

2. What is it costing you? If nothing, they are gone.

3. Can I make a reel out of you? A line, a look, an entry, a needle-drop. If the answer is no, the film does not exist on the platforms where they live.

08Two films that cracked it from opposite ends

Saiyaara — sincerity as a shock tactic

Mohit Suri's film opened 18 July 2025 with two newcomers, a Gulf News review of 2.5 stars, and no star system. It did ₹270.75 Cr net in twelve days, the second-highest opening weekend of the year behind Chhaava, and became, per Gulf News, the highest-grossing love story in Indian cinema. Overseas its second weekend doubled its first and out-sold a superhero franchise released the same frame.

What happened is well documented and the trade spent weeks arguing about whether it was real. It was. Young viewers cried, filmed themselves crying, and posted it. Roughly 200,000 reels and shorts were cut from its scenes and soundtrack. Clinical psychologists quoted in the Indian press described the film as a trigger rather than a cause — it had given a generation raised to be emotionally cautious permission to feel something in public, and they took it.

The analytical reading, which Pinkvilla laid out and we agree with: contrast bias. In a feed of ironic, fast, emotionally shallow content, a sincere, still, melancholic love story stood out "like a quiet cry in a crowded room." The audience remembered it because it hurt. Then the IKEA effect: every reel they cut, every edit they made, was an act of emotional authorship that made the film partly theirs. Bollywood had stopped making intense romance — it had pivoted to thrillers, sanitised rom-coms, spectacle — and scarcity raised the value of the one film that did.

Exhibitor Vishek Chauhan's line to THR India is the one to remember: "You have to embrace it, not resist it. This is the generation we have to cater to now since they're driving the box office."

Dhurandhar — scale, moral grey, and a character you could meme

Aditya Dhar's espionage film took ₹1,144 Cr India net and 3.5 billion hours on Netflix. Its sequel did ₹124 Cr on opening day including paid previews, and $28.56M in North America. It was A-rated, brutally violent, and accused by some critics of being propaganda. Gen Z did not care about the last part.

What they cared about: an undercover protagonist who carries "the psychological cost of operating inside enemy systems"; an antagonist, Rehman Dakait, who is "dangerous and morally grey" with "humanity written into him" and a family; a mentor figure modelled on Ajit Doval; and music that became "part of the film's larger cultural afterlife" — an entry theme you could cut to, an Arijit track that softened the world. Dhurandhar is Uri's "How's the josh?" instinct scaled up: cinematic shorthand that Gen Z converts into "captions, edits and identity." Its soundtrack featured Reble, a rapper from the North East with an Atlantic Records deal, writing lines about bad girls in run-down cities. The film sounded like the people watching it.

What the two have in common

Opposite genres, opposite certificates, opposite budgets. Both had a soundtrack that existed as a product before the film did. Both had at least one character with a visible cost. Both generated hundreds of thousands of user-made clips because there was something in them worth clipping. Neither was afraid of being too much. That is the pattern.

09What Bollywood still has that the alternatives do not

This is the part that tends to get lost in the hand-wringing. The alternatives each win on an axis. None of them has all of the following, and Bollywood — when it remembers — has all of them at once.

  • The song. Anime has openings. K-drama has OSTs. Hollywood has scores. None of them has a three-minute track that can be released a month early, go to 400 million views, and be cut into 200,000 reels before the film opens. This is Bollywood's unique distribution advantage and half the industry treats it as an afterthought.
  • The communal room. Gen Z is now the most frequent cinemagoing cohort in the US, explicitly because of the shared experience. Anime and K-drama are consumed on a phone under a duvet. Bollywood is built for a crowd that whistles at an entry.
  • Indian faces, Indian specificity. Madhavan's son may prefer anime, but he cannot see himself in it. Dhurandhar's Karachi, Saiyaara's Mumbai, Stree 2's Chanderi — the specificity of place is something no import can offer.
  • Scale on the big screen. Spider-Man proved Indian Gen Z will pay for premium formats. Dhurandhar proved a Hindi film can fill them. The audience is not anti-spectacle. It is anti-spectacle-without-a-pulse.
  • Melodrama as a native language. The thing Bollywood was embarrassed about for fifteen years — the big feeling, the operatic heartbreak, the hero who cries — is exactly what Saiyaara proved the audience was starving for. Anime does it. K-drama does it. Bollywood invented it and then tried to be cool instead.

The audience did not outgrow Bollywood. Bollywood, for a decade, tried to outgrow the things the audience loved it for.

10The Boxoffy read: twelve things to change on Monday

  1. Treat the first single as the first release. Plan its YouTube and Instagram life as carefully as the film's. It is the film's opening weekend, four weeks early.
  2. Write the antagonist as well as the hero. Rehman Dakait outlived Hamza in the discourse. The character with the most visible cost wins the reels.
  3. Give the hero something to lose, and let it show. Stoicism reads as absence. The audience has normalised being not-okay; let the protagonist be.
  4. Commit to a tone and hold it. The "vibe" is the whole contract. Break it for an item song and you have broken the film.
  5. Stop writing youth dialogue from the outside. Hire people under 28 in the room, and let them veto. Cringe is detectable in seconds and fatal.
  6. Engineer the clippable moment on purpose. An entry, a needle-drop, a line. If the film cannot be cut into a 15-second reel by a fan, it does not exist where the audience lives.
  7. Market on YouTube, Instagram and BookMyShow, in that order. Television is fourth. Spend accordingly.
  8. Design for groups. This audience goes in threes and fours. Group offers, shared-seat booking, anything that lowers the coordination cost.
  9. Fight the exhibitor on F&B, not ticket price. The ticket is absorbed. The ₹400 popcorn is the thing they resent, and it is your opening weekend it suppresses.
  10. Book premium formats for films that deserve them, and earn it. Spider-Man's English-version dominance is the proof that this audience will pay for the format. Do not put a talky drama in IMAX.
  11. Be sincere or be spectacular. Do not be mild. Saiyaara and Dhurandhar are the two films that worked with this cohort in a year. They have nothing in common except that neither was afraid of being too much.
  12. Stop apologising for melodrama. It is the house style. The competitors are using it. The audience wants it. Bollywood is the only party in the room that seems embarrassed by it.

The one-line version

India's Gen Z is the largest young audience on earth, it is now the most theatrically active cohort in the markets that measure it, and it decides your opening day. It is not asking Bollywood to become anime. It is asking Bollywood to stop being half-hearted.

Caveats. Several screen-time and reading figures are global or US-weighted where India-specific equivalents do not exist; these are labelled. Deloitte's India Gen Z sample is 506 working adults, not a national youth sample. TOBAR covers urban regular Hindi cinema-goers only. The "vibe / drip / cringe" decoding is Boxoffy's editorial reading of the vocabulary, not survey data. Where we characterise what the audience "wants," we are synthesising the above, and we say so.
